v2_s1a.what_it_shows: Grain offered by arrow to a seller, with shoes below.
v2_s1a.missing: Seller rejecting the grain with a crossed-out offer arrow.
v2_s1a.point: Barter fails when seller rejects offered goods

v2_s1s.what_it_shows: Wheat shop with people and signs reading 1 metre cloth and 10 kg wheat.
v2_s1s.missing: Wheat sacks and a cloth roll passing between two people, with exchange arrows.

v2_s1b.what_it_shows: Wheat and a shirt linked by a two-way arrow, with money crossed out.
v2_s1b.missing: A contrasting wheat-to-money-to-shirt exchange marked as not barter.
v2_s1b.point: Barter exchanges directly without money; Money-mediated exchange is not barter; Direct exchange identifies barter

v2_s2.what_it_shows: Wheat and cloth exchanged along opposing arrows, with a handshake and crossed-out money symbol.
v2_s2.missing: A service exchanged for goods, with both people agreeing to the trade.
v2_s2.point: No money does not mean free; Barter includes services; Both parties agree on value

v2_s3.what_it_shows: A grain stalk and a thread spool; a Hindi caption says matching needs makes swapping easy.
v2_s3.missing: A past-to-present timeline showing people exchanging grain and thread, with money and barter used side by side today.
v2_s3.point: Barter अतीत से आज तक बचा है; जरूरतों का मेल swap आसान करता है; पैसा और barter साथ रह सकते हैं

v2_s4s.what_it_shows: A grocery storefront with a sugar bag and floating coins; subtitles describe failed exchanges.
v2_s4s.missing: A comparison showing rejected wheat-for-goods barter versus wheat sold for money, then money used to buy goods from a willing seller.
v2_s4s.point: Exchange succeeds only with a willing seller; Both parties must want each other's goods; Money separates selling from buying

v2_s4b.what_it_shows: Scales, a cow and crops with crosses, plus a calendar and shopping basket, suggest barter difficulties.
v2_s4b.missing: A barter sequence showing mismatched wants, an indivisible cow, spoiling stored crops and a disputed future repayment.
v2_s4b.point: Barter में मूल्य, विभाजन, संग्रह और भुगतान की मुश्किलें; आसान monetary accounting, पर स्थिर purchasing power नहीं; Barter की बाधाएँ matching से repayment तक

v2_s5a.what_it_shows: Arrow-linked evolution from barter to commodity, metallic, paper, bank and digital money; wheat exchanged for a shirt below.

v2_s5s.what_it_shows: Grocery shop with ₹300 price and ₹500 note crossed out above ₹200.
v2_s5s.missing: Two linked exchanges showing salt used as intermediary, and counted coins exchanged for grain.
v2_s5s.point: Salt intermediates two exchanges; Commodity money bridges exchange; Counted coins pay for grain

v2_s5b.what_it_shows: Six illustrated money stages linked by arrows, from barter to digital money.
v2_s5b.missing: A UPI transfer between bank deposits, with coexisting cash and cards shown as access tools rather than money stores.
v2_s5b.point: Easier exchange; UPI transfers existing deposits; Forms coexist; cards need not store money; Six stages in the book's evolution sequence

v2_s6.what_it_shows: Table contrasts intrinsic material value with extrinsic value backed by government and trust.
v2_s6.missing: Side-by-side salt and a paper note, showing salt's practical use versus the note's negligible material worth and institutional backing.
v2_s6.point: Where the two values come from; Useful salt versus negligible paper worth; Material versus institutional source

v2_s7s.what_it_shows: An empty grocery storefront and a person outside.
v2_s7s.missing: Salt packets being used to season food after being received as payment.

v2_s7b.what_it_shows: Salt linked to a shopping basket and food bowl; usefulness icon crossed out.
v2_s7b.missing: Salt shown seasoning food even when it is not accepted as payment.
v2_s7b.point: Intrinsic value exists outside monetary use; Usefulness and purchasing power alone are insufficient; Commodity remains useful beyond payment

v2_s8a.what_it_shows: Commodity–region table for salt, cattle and cowries, with a shell and decorative icons.
v2_s8a.missing: A regional map showing cowries used as money, plus tea bricks and tobacco in their respective regions.
v2_s8a.point: Salt’s regions; cattle’s pastoral communities; Accepted cowries served as money across regions; Tea bricks and tobacco had distinct regional uses

v2_s8s.what_it_shows: Bazaar weighing scale with labels for 2 metres of cloth, 10 kg grain and 2 kg salt.
v2_s8s.missing: An exchange diagram showing all three quantities as equal in value, with two successive exchange arrows passing through salt.
v2_s8s.point: Three quantities have equal assumed value; Salt mediates two successive exchanges

v2_s8b.what_it_shows: Table of commodity money and regions, with egg, salt and cow icons.
v2_s8b.missing: A salt-mediated exchange between people with mismatched wants, showing salt's everyday use and acceptance by both.
v2_s8b.point: Salt bridges mismatched wants; Commodities have uses beyond payment; Usefulness needs community acceptance

v2_s9s.what_it_shows: Grain icon with 100 kg crossed out and 90 kg below, beside a later-payment calendar and question mark.
v2_s9s.missing: A spoiled 10 kg portion separated from the original grain, leaving 90 kg for later payment.
v2_s9s.point: Spoilage reduces grain available for later payment

v2_s9b.what_it_shows: Cattle, transport and weighing icons; crossed-out scales lead to repeated checking and bargaining.
v2_s9b.missing: A commodity splitting or spoiling, with added transport and negotiation costs shown visually.
v2_s9b.point: Commodity money has several practical limitations; Variation and absent standards require repeated negotiation; Division, spoilage and hauling create extra costs

v4_s1a.what_it_shows: ₹100 note icon, grain and gold with question marks, and a handshake.
v4_s1a.missing: A linked diagram showing what ₹100 buys, whether gold backs it, and its legal acceptance for payment.
v4_s1a.point: Purchasing power, gold backing, and legal status questioned

v4_s1s.what_it_shows: Bank counter, customer and a large '1 note' card.
v4_s1s.missing: An old banknote exchanged for gold, contrasted with a modern rupee note that cannot be redeemed for gold.
v4_s1s.point: Old gold redemption, not today's rupee

v4_s1b.what_it_shows: Paper currency points to gold; paper material is crossed out; a handshake marks redemption promise, with a receipt–goods analogy.
v4_s1b.missing: A holder exchanging a note for gold under an explicit redemption promise, contrasted with gold reserves without a claim.
v4_s1b.point: Value comes from redeemability, not paper; Gold reserves alone do not establish a claim; Redemption promise explains the need for backing

v4_s2s.what_it_shows: A bank with labels '10 grams' and '10 notes'.
v4_s2s.missing: One extra note paired with one extra gram of gold, added to matching piles.

v4_s2b.what_it_shows: Central bank gold reserves linked by arrows to issued notes, redemption, and gold.
v4_s2b.missing: A shrinking gold reserve limiting note issuance and prompting holders to demand gold when repayment confidence falls.
v4_s2b.point: Reserved gold supports the redemption promise; Gold backing constrains issue and enables qualified redemption; Weaker repayment capacity triggers gold demands

v4_s3.what_it_shows: Receipt scroll, official stamp and banknote icons, with a 1661 Sweden label.
v4_s3.missing: A timeline showing deposited goods becoming receipts, then state-issued claims with compulsory acceptance before Sweden’s 1661 banknotes.
v4_s3.point: Receipts can stand for deposited goods; Deposit claims acquire a state issuer; Compulsory acceptance precedes Sweden's banknotes

v4_s4s.what_it_shows: किराना दुकान, ग्राहक, दुकानदार और ₹100 का संकेत।
v4_s4s.missing: ग्राहक से मिला ₹100 दुकानदार आगे किसी दूसरे विक्रेता को देता और वह स्वीकार करता दिखे।
v4_s4s.point: आगे खर्च होने का भरोसा मुद्रा स्वीकार करवाता है

v4_s4b.what_it_shows: Authority, trust, fiat money and groceries icons with arrows; separate gold-backed paper note.
v4_s4b.missing: A comparison showing redeemable gold-backed paper versus authority-issued fiat, with issuance control and purchasing power.
v4_s4b.point: Authority और trust से purchasing power; Paper form alone does not mean fiat; Gold बिना issuance control का सवाल

v4_s5.what_it_shows: Dollar, euro, yen and yuan symbols linked by arrows, with a question mark.
v4_s5.missing: A causal diagram linking issuing authority and public trust to money’s value, distinguishing printing from authorised issuance, and showing policy rates affecting borrowing and demand.
v4_s5.point: Fiat value rests on authority and trust; Printing differs from authorised issuance; Credit costs transmit policy to demand

v4_s6s.what_it_shows: Shop scene with a ₹10 price tag, coin and banknote; caption says a valid special-design coin clears the debt.
v4_s6s.missing: A payment comparison showing special-design coins accepted, notes without a ceiling, and the compulsory coin-acceptance limit.
v4_s6s.point: Valid currency clears the debt; Valid special-design coins also pay; Notes unrestricted; compulsory coin acceptance has a ceiling

v4_s6b.what_it_shows: Banknote icons, a green check, denominations and a no-ceiling label beside an RBI Act scroll.
v4_s6b.missing: A comparison showing banknotes accepted without a value ceiling versus coins accepted only up to the statutory limit.
v4_s6b.point: Official recognition and circulation use; Valid banknotes have no tender ceiling; Coin acceptance obligation stops at statutory limit

v4_s7a.what_it_shows: Commemorative coin icon with legal-tender, metal-value and collector-value symbols and a red cross.
v4_s7a.missing: A commemorative coin in a protective case contrasted with an everyday coin being spent, with face, metal and collector values distinguished.
v4_s7a.point: Legal tender need not always be fiat; Commemorative coins have separate status and values; Preserving collector condition discourages daily spending

v4_s7s.what_it_shows: Shop scene with a demonetization panel and a ₹0 bill with a downward arrow.
v4_s7s.missing: Withdrawn coins rejected beside an unpaid bill, with coin groups and their tender ceilings shown visually.
v4_s7s.point: Withdrawn coins leave the bill unpaid; Coin groups have different tender ceilings

v4_s7b.what_it_shows: Denomination-by-denomination tender-limit table, coin icons, and a ₹10 limit gauge.
v4_s7b.missing: A comparison showing coin counts versus total value, with collector price separate from legal-tender status.
v4_s7b.point: Value limits are not coin-count limits; Different denominations have different tender rules; Tender limits and collector prices do not change status

v4_s8.what_it_shows: Mining-to-network-to-Bitcoin arrows, a 2024 El Salvador label, and legal and price icons.
v4_s8.missing: A before-and-after payment scene showing compulsory Bitcoin acceptance ending while voluntary acceptance continues, separate from network issuance and market pricing.
v4_s8.point: Payment does not prove government issuance; Legal tender exception, network issuance and market price; Compulsory acceptance ends, voluntary use remains

v4_s9.what_it_shows: One ₹100 coin branches to payment and collection, with silver inspection and a price tag.
v4_s9.missing: A side-by-side comparison showing the same coin worth ₹100 for payment but fetching a higher collector price.
v4_s9.point: Same coin, two roles; Face value differs from collector price; Collector appeal raises price, not denomination

v4_s10s.what_it_shows: Bank, ₹1,000 balance, and a supply–demand balance scale.
v4_s10s.missing: A side-by-side diagram showing a cheque transferring existing deposits between accounts and a credit payment creating new debt.
v4_s10s.point: Cheque से जमा रकम का transfer; Credit payment से नया उधार

v4_s10b.what_it_shows: Cheque and card payment arrows, a bank, and college acceptance marked with a tick.
v4_s10b.missing: A three-column visual separating payment instruments, currency, and legal-tender status.
v4_s10b.point: Payment instruments are not currency or legal status; Separate three concepts; question dollar demand
